thread.title: Finkelman says cheaper insurance needs to be 2026 legislative priority
thread.title_full: Finkelman says cheaper insurance needs to be 2026 legislative priority

author: ohtadmin
title: Finkelman says cheaper insurance needs to be 2026 legislative priority
text:
A Jamestown man who was first elected to office in November 2022 has begun his fourth legislative session in the Rhode Island House of Representatives.
Alex Finkelman, 39, ran uncontested for his District 74 seat, Jamestown and Middletown, in ’22 and 2024. He returned Jan. 7 to Smith Hill in Providence with the aim to make insurance cheaper for homeowners. This fits well with Finkelman’s job as he serves as president of The Egis Group, an insurance firm in Warwick.
“We have a real challenge with homeowner’s insurance,” he said.
Finkelman is crafting a bill to target liability and the replacement cost of the structure, which are two of the major costs. He said it is harder to control the reconstruction cost of a property, but lawmakers can help aid the liability exposure of insurance carriers.
Finkelman said one of his biggest accomplishments of 2025 was a bill he introduced that eliminated restrictions on investments by insurance companies.
The legislation, which was signed into law by Gov. Dan McKee in June, eliminated the statute that limited insurance companies headquartered in Rhode Island from investing any more than 10% of their assets in “Schedule BA” investments These are generally nontraditional long-term investments other than stocks and bonds, such as hedge funds, private equity and fixed-income securities.
“Rhode Island is very fortunate to be home to industry-leading insurers who are among our state’s biggest employers and greatest contributors to our economy,” Finkelman said after introducing the legislation. “This bill lifts a needless restraint so they have the freedom to innovate and grow so they can continue to flourish right here in Rhode Island.”
The policy change was requested by the Johnston insurance firm FM. Finkelman’s bill, which passed unanimously (71-0) in the House, was credited for keeping the employer in Rhode Island.
Finkelman said there “is still a lot of work to do” looking forward to the ’26 session.
“Going back for another year gives me more time to accomplish some of those things I set out to do,” he said.
What he doesn’t expect will be different from 2025 is McKee’s budget.
“We’re looking at another very large deficit,” Finkelman said. “It’s going to be another tough year.”
A new law that went into effect Jan. 1 prohibits students from accessing personal electronic devices, notably cell phones, at school. Finkelman said he “fully supports” the law.
“As a parent with young kids in school, I see how distracting cell phones can be during the day,” he said. “I think this is a commonsense step to protect learning time and classroom focus.”
The General Assembly’s focus on healthcare in ’25 included a $40 million allocation toward Medicaid rate increases for primary care providers and $38 million more for hospital reimbursement rates.
Finkelman said this work is not done. The shortage of primary care doctors in Rhode Island is a challenge when trying to ensure that people have the access to the healthcare they need.
“We need to support funding that protects access to care while understanding that we have a tight budget,” Finkelman said.
Finkelman, who said he relishes the “ability to influence a positive outcome” as a lawmaker, thought Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi’s opening statement “underscored the challenges facing Rhode Island,” including the cost of living. He did credit the speaker, however, for his plea for responsible budgeting and investments when it comes to education and infrastructure.
“As we head into session, I look forward to working with the speaker and my colleagues on practical solutions that make a meaningful difference for our communities,” he said.
